title: Родовое гнездо из спичек  (The Matchstick Ancestral Estate)

segments.t: At the restaurant, sous-chef Lyova carries a large covered box into Chef Barinov's office. His mother's birthday is tomorrow, and since she is doing a deep cleaning of their apartment today, Lyova needs a safe place to hide the intricate matchstick mansion he spent two weeks gluing together.
Шеф, можно я поставлю коробку в кабинете?
Завтра у моей любимой мамы большой юбилей.
Зачем твоей маме дома вторая мультиварка?
Это не мультиварка, а наш старинный дом!
У нашей семьи настоящие дворянские корни.
Наше родовое гнездо сгорело во время войны.
Я решил воссоздать его из обычных спичек.
Лёва, да ты просто настоящий зодчий!
Я целых две недели клеил этот дворец.
Завтра дома уборка, и мама может найти.
Не бойся, поставь свой дворец на стол.
Рыбка Аркадий надёжно посторожит твой подарок!
Let's look at how Lyova explains his fragile matchstick masterpiece to Chef Barinov.
Шеф, можно я поставлю коробку в кабинете?
'Chef, may I put the box in the office?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Lyova's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
Завтра у моей любимой мамы большой юбилей.
'Tomorrow is my beloved mom's big milestone birthday.' Notice how Russian puts 'tomorrow' and 'anniversary' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
Зачем твоей маме дома вторая мультиварка?
'Why does your mom need a second slow cooker at home?' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'what for, why' and finishes on 'cooker', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Это не мультиварка, а наш старинный дом!
'This is not a slow cooker, but our old family house!' Lyova lifts the cover to reveal a miniature architectural model.
У нашей семьи настоящие дворянские корни.
'Our family has real noble roots.' Lyova pairs 'family' with 'roots' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Наше родовое гнездо сгорело во время войны.
'Our ancestral estate burned down during the war.' Notice how Russian puts 'estate' and 'of war' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
Я решил воссоздать его из обычных спичек.
'I decided to recreate it out of ordinary matches.' Here Lyova anchors the thought on 'to decide; to solve' and finishes on 'matches', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Лёва, да ты просто настоящий зодчий!
'Lyova, you are simply a true master builder!' Barinov admires the intricate craftsmanship using an elevated noun for architect.
Я целых две недели клеил этот дворец.
'I glued this palace for two whole weeks.' Lyova pairs 'week' with 'palace' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Завтра дома уборка, и мама может найти.
'Tomorrow there is cleaning at home, and Mom might find it.' Lyova explains why he cannot keep the surprise gift in their apartment.
Не бойся, поставь свой дворец на стол.
'Do not worry, put your palace on the table.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'fear' and finishes on 'table, desk', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Рыбка Аркадий надёжно посторожит твой подарок!
'Arkady the fish will reliably guard your gift!' He jokes that his aquarium fish will watch over the matchstick model. Now let's hear the complete office scene with Lyova and Chef Barinov again.

Chef Barinov promises that his office fish Arkady will guard the matchstick palace, unaware of how flammable matches are around his cigars. See you next time!
До встречи!
